<meta>continues from previous page: [they] flee and shudder at them, such as all <term>Sales</term> <gloss>salts</gloss>. For we see that, if they are cast into the fire, the aqueous spirit breaks out with a crackling sound before the flame is kindled. This also occurs gently in leaves that are somewhat more resistant, as the aqueous part breaks out before the oily part kindles into flame. But this is seen most of all in <term>Argentum vivum</term> <gloss>quicksilver or mercury</gloss>, which is not inappropriately called mineral water. For this, without inflammation, through simple eruption and expansion, almost equals the power of gunpowder; it is even said that, when mixed with gunpowder, it multiplies its power.</meta>

Similarly, let the <term>Natura Inquisita</term> <gloss>nature under inquiry</gloss> be the transitory nature of flame and its momentary extinction. For the nature of flame does not seem to be fixed and consistent here among us, but rather to be generated at almost every moment and immediately extinguished. For it is manifest that, in flames which are continued and endure here, that duration is not of the same flame as an <term>Individuum</term> <gloss>individual entity</gloss>, but occurs through a succession of new flames generated in order, and by no means does the same flame remain in number. This is easily perceived from the fact that, once the fuel or combustible material of the flame is withdrawn, the flame perishes immediately. The <term>Bivium</term> <gloss>crossroads or twofold path</gloss> regarding this nature is such: this momentary nature is either caused by the cessation of the cause that first generated it, as in light, sounds, and so-called violent motions; or it is because the flame could remain in its nature here among us, but is

<summary>This page explores the physical properties of substances like salts and mercury, noting how aqueous components affect combustion, and investigates the transitory, non-persistent nature of flames.</summary>
<keywords>Flame, Combustion, Mercury, Gunpowder, Transitory nature, Physics</keywords>
